row.name: Nakhchivan Rock Signs
row.description: The Nakhchivan Rock Signs were discovered in 2016 at Agsal, between the villages of Erefse and Milax in the Culfa (Julfa) region of Azerbaijan [1] [2]. Three rock signs were found featuring drainage channels directed towards the canyon, suggesting fluid flow [1]. Similar rock signs are common across Southern Azerbaijan and Eastern Anatolia [1] [3].

row.name: Rudna Glava
row.description: One of the earliest copper mines in Europe, dating to the 5th millennium BC in eastern Serbia [1]. Excavations by Borislav Jovanovic (1968-1986) uncovered mine shafts following veins of copper ore, some extending 15-20 metres into the hillside [2] [3] [4]. Miners used fire-setting and thermal shock techniques to fracture rock [3] [4]. Vincha culture pottery from the Gradac phase confirms the chronology [3] [4]. Added to Serbia's Archaeological Sites of Exceptional Importance in 1983 [1] [5].

row.name: Banwolseong
row.description: Wolseong or Wolseong Palace was a royal palace of Silla [1]. It was located in what is now Gyeongju [1]. The palace was used during the Silla and Unified Silla periods [1]. The palace gets its names from the approximate outline of the palace walls, which were shaped like a crescent moon [1]. It is also called Banwolseong or Sinwolseong or Jaeseong, which means where the king resides [1]. The South Korean government has also designated the palace ruins as Historic Site No. 16 [1].

row.name: Seahenge
row.description: Seahenge, also known as Holme I, was a prehistoric monument located in the village of Holme-next-the-Sea, near Old Hunstanton in the English county of Norfolk [1]. A timber circle with an upturned tree root in the centre, Seahenge, along with the nearby timber circle Holme II, was built in the spring-summer of 2049 BC [1]. The site consisted of an outer ring comprising 55 small split oak trunks forming a roughly circular enclosure around 7 by 6 metres [1]. Rather than being placed in individual holes, the timbers had been arranged around a circular construction trench [1]. Their split sides faced inwards and their bark faced outwards (with one exception where the opposite is the case) [1]. One of the trunks on the south western side had a narrow Y fork in it, permitting access to the central area [1]. Seahenge was originally constructed on a salt marsh, and over the centuries the area became a freshwater wetland, as an offshore barrier grew up, preventing sea water from getting access to the area around the circle [1].

row.old_value: Built around 90 AD. The Main Limes used the River Main as a 50 km natural barrier reinforced by watchtowers. Part of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes — now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A 3.2 km megalithic avenue of stones linking stone circles and burial mounds, built 3000–2000 BC. One of only three such complexes in the region.
row.new_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.

row.old_value: A cylindrical limestone obelisk from the Early Neolithic with a faint spiral engraving. It was once part of a group of nine; only two survive today.
row.new_value: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos.

row.old_value: From around 10,000 BC, Aboriginal people hunted wallaby in open tundra near Kutikina Cave on the Franklin River. This Pleistocene rock shelter helped establish the antiquity of Tasmanian occupation.
row.new_value: Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness.

row.old_value: Doric stoa from around 500 BC, seat of the Archon Basileus and repository of Athenian law. Incoming magistrates swore their oaths on a sacred stone kept within its walls.
row.new_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.

row.new_value: Walls shaped like a crescent moon gave Banwolseong its name: a royal palace of Silla in what is now Gyeongju, used through both the Silla and Unified Silla periods.

row.old_value: An oval-shaped broch from 150 BC that originally stood on a freshwater lake island. Walls survive 4.5 metres high, and the sea now laps at its foundations.
row.new_value: Now on an exposed promontory of South Uist, but originally on a freshwater lake, the oval Iron Age broch of Dun Vulan still has walls standing 4.5 metres high and 4 metres wide.

row.old_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.
row.new_value: In the northwestern corner of the Athenian Agora stood Stoa Basileios, among the smallest known Greek stoas, yet it kept Athens' laws and the stone on which new magistrates swore their oath.

row.old_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.
row.new_value: In the Eden Valley, Shap Stone Avenue ends at a burial cairn, Skellaw Hill. Its Goggleby Stone, cup-marked on its north face, led Tom Clare to suggest a Late Neolithic date.

row.old_value: A Roman fish farm from 146 BC with a connecting aqueduct carved into coastal rock. Romans engineered saltwater ponds to breed fish on an industrial scale.
row.new_value: East of Santa Eulària des Riu on Ibiza, S'Argamassa Roman Fish Farm keeps remains of rectangular tanks where garum once fermented, before amphoras carried it to all parts of the empire.

row.old_value: An Iron Age trade route crossing the Cotswolds, linking the Thames to the Severn. The Romans later upgraded it to connect their major roads Akeman Street and the Fosse Way.
row.new_value: The Welsh Way, a British Iron Age trade route across the Cotswold Hills, links the highest navigable point on the Thames at Lechlade to the lowest crossing of the Severn at Gloucester.

row.old_value: A timber circle from 2049 BC with an upturned oak tree root at its centre. The upside-down tree may symbolise a world turned on its head — death itself.

row.old_value: 5th-millennium BC copper mine with shafts cut into the hillside and scaffolding for ore access — among the earliest evidence of European copper mining. Pottery links it firmly to the Vinča culture.
row.new_value: Miners here broke the rock with fire-setting and thermal shock. Shafts follow veins of copper ore, some 15-20 metres into the hillside, in one of the earliest copper mines in Europe.

row.old_value: Walls shaped like a crescent moon gave Banwolseong its name: a royal palace of Silla in what is now Gyeongju, used through both the Silla and Unified Silla periods.
row.new_value: A crescent moon: that is the rough outline of this royal palace's walls. The palace takes its names from that shape, and one more name means where the king resides.
